M Khaled Ahmed, Advocate with Md Munir Hossain, Advocate -----For Opposite-Party No. 1

full_judgment:
On 10-4-2011, opposite-party No.1 as complainant instituted a petition of Complaint against the accused-petitioners and others in the Court of Senior Judicial Magistrate, Borlekha, Moulvibazar alleging, inter- alia, that the complainant is a businessman of agar-attar, who would export agar-attar to the different countries of Middle-East maintaining a shop in Arab-Emirat for that purpose. He had been dealing in the said business in Dubai and Bangladesh since 1990-2002 and his two brothers would also reside in Arab-Emirat for business purposes. Before going to Dubai, he had a close relationship with accused Nos. 1 and 2. While the complainant was staying in Dubai, accused NO.2 went to Dubai. On the advantage of earlier relationship, accused No.1 requested the complainant to include accused No. 2 in the agar-attar business as a result the complainant involved accused No. 2 in the business. On a request and good faith, the complainant started providing agar-attar to accused Nos. 1 and 2 since 1996-2002 on the assurance that they would pay up the price of agar-altar in Dubai alter selling the same. Since the complainant supplied agar-attar to accused Nos. 1 and 2 since 1996-2002, the" price of agar-attar to the tune of 1,16,490 Dirham equivalent to Taka 23,00,677.50 remained overdue, In order to make payment against the outstanding dues, accused Nos.1 and 2 issued a number of cheques of Standard Chartered Bank and City Bank, Dera Branch of Dubai; but the afore-said cheques presented before the bank for encashment were dishonored for insufficient fund. 'In 2002, before coming over Bangladesh, the complainant requested accused No.2 for payment of the outstanding dues. In reply, accused No. 2 told that he would send money to his brother accused No. 1 in Bangladesh and then he would pay the money to the complainant in Bangladesh. The complainant, thereafter, talked with accused No. lover telephone about payment of the outstanding dues. However, accused No. 1 assured the complainant of payment of all outstanding dues in Bangladesh and requested the complainant not to preach their bad names' abroad. Upon believing accused No. 1 and 2, the complainant came to Bangladesh and demanded outstanding dues to accused No. 1 who gained time upon several assurances. In such a situation, the complainant talked to accused No. 2 over telephone in Dubai buthe gave assurance to send Money from Dubai and gained time telling this and that. Accused No. 2 came to Bangladesh before the second date of occurrence. The complainant coming over Bangladesh again demanded the outstanding dues from accused Nos. I and 2 but they disclosed that accused No. 2 had come to the country for settlement of his marriage but the marriage would be unsettled if gold worth Taka 3 lakh would not be given to the bride's party. They also requested the complainant saying that if the complainant would not give Taka 2 lakhto them, the marriage of accused No.2 would not be performed and in that case, their prestige would be highly tarnished. Accused No. 1 and 2, dishonestly induced the complainant by saying that the entire outstanding dues along with the loan amount of Taka 2 lakh would be given to him within 2 months. ; Upon good faith to the proposal of accused and with the hope of getting back of earlier outstanding dues of Taka 23,00,677.50, the complainant on the 2nd date of occurrence following 21-8-2010 delivered Taka 2 lakh as loan to accused Nos. 1 and 2 who received the same at the place of occurrence. After two months, the complainant again demanded his out standing dues along with the loan amount to accused No. I who on hearing the complainant became very furious and refused to pay up the loan money and gave threat of killing by using kirish if the money would be further demanded. The complainant informed the local chairman and member of the matter. After informing the local chairman and member of the matter, accused No. 1 with the help of accused No.3 started giving threat in different times and gave intimidation of killing. The complainant informed the local elders of the fact, who assured him of the settlement of the dispute. However, the complainant was threatened with killing by the accused-petitioners who disclosed that if the complainant would claim the money again they would kill him and throw his dead body in the nearby jungle. Alter disclosing threat of dire consequences, the accused denied all monetary transaction and refused to payoff the loan amount to the complainant. It is alleged in the petition of complaint that the accused of the case look the loan amount from the complainant by making allurement on him and took the aforesaid money by deception inducing the complainant fraudulently and dishonestly with initial intention to deceive the complainant. Hence, the petition of complainant against the accused-petitioner and another under sections 406/420/506/109 of the Penal Code. 

 3. On receipt of he petition of complaint, the learned Senior Judicial Magistrate; Borlekha examined the complainant under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and took cognizance of the offences against the accused-petitioners and others under sections 406/420/506/109 of the Penal Cede and issued summons directing them to appear before the Court. Subsequently, an order of arrest and P&A were also issued against the accused-petitioners and others. Accused-petitioner No. 1 and 3 approached this Court with an application for anticipatory bail whereupon High Court Division by order dated 20-6-2011 granted anticipatory bail to the petitioners for a period of 4 months in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 16470 of 20I1. 

 5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned proceedings, the accused-petitioners approached this Court with an application under section 561A of Code of Criminal Procedure with a view to quashing the impugned proceedings and obtained this Rule and order of stay of all further proceedings of the case. 

 6. At the very outset, Mr Nirmulendu Dev, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioners, submits that the allegations that have been disclosed in the petition of complaint even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not disclose offences against the accused-petitioners under sections 406/420/506/109 of the Penal Code and this being the stale of affairs, the impugned proceedings should be quashed. He next submits that the allegations that have been leveled against the accused-petitioners may, at the best, be civil disputes which are arisen out of long term business transaction between the complainant and the accused since 1996-2002 and from this standpoint, the initiation and continuation of the impugned proceedings against the accused-petitioners are wholly ex- facie illegal and not tenable in the eye of law and considering that aspect of the case, the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioners are liable to be quashed. Learned Advocate, in support of his contentions, referred to the cases of Syed Ali Mir vs Syed Omar Ali reported in 10 BCR (AD) 287 = 42 DLR (AD) 240 and Islam Ali Mia alias Md Islam vs Amal Chandra Mondal reported in 45 DLR (AD) 27. He then submits that since the alleged offences arising out of business transaction occurred outside Bangladesh, that offences are not triable by any competent Criminal Court in Bangladesh in view of section 177 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and in that view of the matter, the impugned proceedings are also not sustainable in the eye of law. He candidly submits that the alleged Allegations which have been leveled" against the accused-petitioners are preposterous and absurd story which are nothing but continuation of either dispute arising out of business transaction during 1996-2002 and that the alleged story of taking loan of Taka 2,00,000 in spite of earlier outstanding dues arising out of business transaction cannot be a believable story by a man of ordinary prudence and, as such, the story of giving loan to the tune of Taka 2,00,000 to the accused-petitioners in Bangladesh despite the previous outstanding dues is preposterous and absurd fact which is not at all believable by any person of ordinary prudence and, as such, the impugned proceedings are totally, illegal and unjust and the same should be' quashed outright by this Court invoking its jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Learned Advocate, in support of his contentions, relied on the ease of Md Shams uddin alias Lambu vs State reported in 8 BLD (AD) 93= 40 DLR (AD) 69. He lastly submits that the accused-petitioners after obtaining anticipatory bail on 20-6- 2011 filed this instant application under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that the period of anticipatory bail expired during pendency of this criminal miscellaneous case and in such a posture of things, the accused-petitioners are entitled to prosecute the Rule and they are entitled to get relief in the Rule. He further submits that since the accused-petitioners after filing an application under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure obtained stay order from this Court, they could not surrender before die' concerned Court below and pray for regular bail there from. He lastly submits that the accused-petitioners have filed an application for bail in this Rule and considering that aspect of the case, it cannot be said that the accused-petitioners approached this Court with unclean hands and this being the position of the case, the accused-petitioners cannot be fugitive from justice and in that view of the matter, the application filed under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the accused-petitioners is competent and maintainable in the eye of law. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr M Khaled Ahmed, learned Advocate along with Mr Md Munir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of complainant-opposite-party No.1, submits that the allegations which have been brought against the accused-petitioners prima-facie disclose of fences against them under sections 06/420/506/109 of the Penal Code and in that view of the matter, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. He next submits that though the complainant had business relationship with the accused-petitioners during the period from 1996- 2002, the complainant being fraudulently allured by the accused-petitioners gave Taka 2,00,000 to the accused-petitioners with the hope that the accused-petitioners would pay the entire previous outstanding dues along with the present loan amount of Taka 2,00,000 to the complainant; but the accused denied all the monetary transaction and refused to pay off the loan amount and in that view of the matter, there are prima-facie allegations of initial deception of taking loan of Taka 200,000 from the complainant which very much attract the ingredients of section 420 of the Penal Code. Learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1, in support of his submissions, relied on the cases of Siddique Abedin vs Md Musa Alum and State reported in 54 DLR 506 and Nurul Islam vs State, reported in 49 DLR 464. He then submits that the accused-petitioners were enlarged on anticipatory bail on 20-6-2011 for a period of 4 months which expired on 19-10-2011 and the accused-petitioners obtained the Instant Rule under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 23-8-2011; but at present, they are fugitive from Justice as no regular bail was obtained by them after the expiry of the period of said anticipatory bail. Under the circumstances, the accused-petitioners are not entitled to prosecute the Rule and that there is no scope to consider the case on merit and this being the scenario of the case, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. Learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1, in support of his contentions, referred to a decision in the case of Mansur Ali (Md) vs State reported in 55. DLR (AD) 131. He lastly submits that refusal to give the loan amount to the complainant does not ordinarily give rise to criminal prosecution but if the money is taken by allurement taking malafide mind in order to defraud the complainant, that may lead to the allegation of criminal offence under section 420 of the Penal Code and in that view of the matter, there is no bar to proceeding with the criminal case notwithstanding the fact that a civil suit has been filed for the recovery, of loan amount in civil Court as both the civil suit and the criminal ease can proceed together and considering that aspect of the case, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. 

 10. In view of the submissions and counter-submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the respective parties, an important question arises as to whether the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioners should be quashed. In order to come to a decision on this point, it will be necessary to see the extent of the principles and categories of cases in which the High Court Division may invoke its extra-ordinary power and authority under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing a proceeding. In the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, reported in 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16, it has been spelt out that to bring a case within the purview of section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the purpose of quashing a proceeding, one of the following conditions must be fulfilled:- 

 (1) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so pre- posterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused, 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FIR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 11. It is pertinent to note that inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be invoked at any stage of the proceedings even after conclusion of the trial, if it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In the case of Sher Ali (Md) vs State, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67, it has been decided:- 

 "(i) There should be fraudulent of dishonest inducement of a person by deceiving him; (ii)(a) the person so deceived-should be induced to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property; or (b) the person so deceived should be intentionally induced to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived; and (iii) in cases covered by (ii)(b), the act or omission should be one which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to the person induced in body, mind, reputation or property. (Ram Das vs State of UP, AIR 1974 SC 1811). 

 16. Now, we want to discuss whether the petition of complaint discloses prima facie offence of cheating against the accused-petitioners in the instant case. On a bare reading of the petition of complaint, we find that there was a business transaction of agar-attar between the complainant and the accused during 1996-2002. While there was a business transaction between the parties, an amount of Taka 23,00,677.50 remained overdue. It also transpires from the petition of complaint that in order to make payment against the outstanding dues, the accused-petitioner issued a number of cheques which were, subsequently, dishonored for insufficient fund. However, when the complainant came to Bangladesh, accused-petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 went to him and demanded Taka 2,00,000 as loan on condition that they would pay up the entire outstanding dues along; with present loan at a time after two months. From the petition of complaint, it transpires that the accused-petitioners subsequently denied all he transaction of loan amount and gave him threat of killing. From the averments made in the petition of complaint, a prima-facie case of cheating following deception of obtaining loan money by the accused-petitioners has been made out. It may be noted here that ordinarily criminal proceedings do not arise to prosecute a person when there is a breach of terms and conditions of contract; but the elements which convert the breach of contract into an offence of cheating is the dishonest or fraudulent intention of the accused at the time he induces the complainant to enter into the written or verbal contract. 

 18. In the case of Siddique Abedin vs Md Musa A/am and State reported in 54 DLR 506 adverted to by the learned Advocate for opposite- party No. 1, it has been held:- "As the money was taken after giving a specific promise of returning it within a specified time the failure to pay the money attracts the offence of cheating. The proceedings cannot be quashed." 

 19. Similar view, on this point, has been expressed in the case of Nurul Islam vs State, reported in 49 DLR 464 relied on by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No.1, wherein it has been decided :- 

 21. We have gone through the decision taken in the case of Syed Ali Mir vs Syed Omar Ali reported in 10 BCR 1990 (AD) 287 = 42 DLR (AD) 240 referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, wherein it has been laid down:- 

 (c) The impugned proceeding is misconceived. 

 22. It is true that non-payment of money fallen due in course of business transaction docs not give rise to criminal prosecution; but when any accused fraudulently or dishonestly induced any person to deliver any property to him with an intention to deceive the complainant or informant may very much fall within the ambit of cheating as defined in section 415 of the Penal Code. Aside from this, it is now well-settled that a criminal ease may he filed for criminal liability provided the ingredients of the offences arc present and a civil suit may be field for civil liability provided there arc causes of action for filing of the same. Both the civil suit and the criminal case can proceed against the accused-petitioners and others. For instance, we may refer to the ease of Khondaker Abu Bashar vs State, 63 DLR (AD) 79, wherein it has been, decided :- 

 "There is no legal impediment to file a criminal case even if a civil suit is pending on the selfsame allegations provided the ingredients of the offences are present." 

 23. Similar view on this point, has also been expressed in the case of Khondakar Mahtabuddin Ahmed vs State, 49 DLR (AD) 132, wherein it has been laid down:- 

 "There is nothing in law precluding a criminal case on account of a civil suit pending against the petitioners on same facts. The criminal case stands for the offence, while civil suit for realization of money. Both can stand together. 

 24. Under the circumstances and the propositions of law, we are of the view that there is no legal bar to proceeding with the criminal case against the accused-petitioners even if a civil suit is pending or a civil suit is filed for realization of loan money. 

 25. On the facts and in the circumstances of the ease, the. decisions taken in the cases of Islam Ali Mia alias Md Islam vs Amal Chandra Mandai, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 27 and Md. Shamsuddin alias Lambu vs State, reported in 8 BLD (AD) 93 = 40 DLR (AD) 69 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners do not appear to be applicable to the instant proceedings as the facts and circumstances of the reported case are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 31. It is alleged by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1 that the criminal miscellaneous case filed under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not maintainable and the same is incompetent as the accused-petitioners, at present, are fugitive from justice since they do not obtain regular bail from the concerned Court below after expiry of anticipatory bail. 

 32. We have stated earlier that the accused- petitioners were enlarged on anticipatory bail on 20-6-2011. After obtaining anticipatory bail, the accused-petitioners approached this Court with an application tinder section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure with a view to quashing the impugned proceedings. It may be mentioned that the accused-petitioners obtained anticipatory bail after taking cognizance of the offence against them. It may be noted that after submission of the police report, there is no scope for granting anticipatory bailor pre-arrest bail to the accused of the case. Though the accused-petitioner filed this miscellaneous case remaining on anticipatory bail, but during pendency of the instant Rule, the period of anticipatory bail expired and in that view of the matter, the accused-petitioners became fugitive from justice. In the case of State vs Wahab Mia reported in 51 DLR (AD) 242, it has been held :- 

 "Anticipatory bail should be granted by the High Court Division for a limited period or till filing of the charge-sheet whichever is appropriate in the circumstances of the case. After expiry of the period or filing of the charge-sheet, as the case may he, the accused must appear before the Court concerned and obtain fresh bail from the Court on the merit of the case." 

 33. The aforesaid view finds support in the case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Mahmud Hossain, 61 DLR (AD) 17, wherein it was observed in paragraph No. 13 as under :- 

 "Even in our jurisdiction this principle is always adhered to and was never deviated from, as because -this convention or principle has been a norm maintained in our criminal jurisprudence to affect the audience or appearance of the accused in reply to any process of the Court. This has become very much a practice and procedure in our Criminal jurisprudence that a person in obedience to a process of the Court must surrender before the Court and challenge the alleged action against him. In the instant case, the petitioner having not surrendered to the process of the Court could not file any application or put his grievance before a Court of law, far less before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Thus, in the absence of any surrender before the process of law, the Court of law is incompetent to issue any order or say any process at its behest and if done so that would be illegal and without jurisdiction and, as such, this petition is not maintainable." 

 35. From the decision made in the case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs ATM Nazimulla Chowdhury 62 DLR (AD) 225, it is now well-settled that when a person wants to seek remedy from a Court of law, he is required to submit to the due process of the Court and unless he surrenders to the jurisdiction of the Court, the Court will not pass any order in his aid. 

 36. In the instant case, the accused-petitioner filed the present criminal case remaining on anticipatory bail but the period of anticipatory bail expired during pendency of the present Rule and they became fugitive after 19-10-2011. The accused-petitioners did not obtain regular bail after expiry of the period of anticipatory bail and, as such, they become fugitive from the proceedings in the eye of law. However, they have appealed before this Court and submitted an application for bail explaining their position that they could not surrender before the concerned Court below due to stay order passed by a Division Bench of this Court. Learned Advocate for the petitioners points out that the accused- petitioners are not at fault rather it is the fault of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, who could not provide proper advice to the accused- petitioners in this regard. 

 37. It may be noted that the accused-petitioners were enlarged on anticipatory bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 16470 of 2011 for a period of 4 (four) months and the application for anticipatory bail was disposed of on 20-6-2011 and that application for anticipatory bail is no more pending before this Court. On the other hand, though the accused-petitioners filed this miscellaneous case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal. Procedure and obtained Rule along with the order of stay of all further proceedings of CR No. 57 of 2011 but no bail was granted to the accused-petitioners in the instant Rule. Since the Rule is going to be disposed of by this judgment, there is no scope to enlarge the accused-petitioners on bail in this Rule. However, they may be directed to appear before the concerned Court below and to seek regular bail there from. Since we find that the accused-petitioners are fugitive from the proceedings, the accused- petitioners are not entitled to prosecute the Rule on that account. 

 38. From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, we are led to hold that the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioners under sections 406/420/506/109 of the Penal Code cannot be quashed and that the same are very much maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law. 

 39. Having considered all the aspects of the case, we do not find any merit in this Rule. Accordingly, the Rule fails. 

 41. The accused-petitioners are directed to surrender before the concerned Court below within 07 (seven) days from the date of receipt of this judgment by the learned Senior Judicial Magistrate, Borlekha, Moulvibazar who shall be at liberty to consider the application for bail on the merit of the case if they surrender before the concerned Court below and pray for regular bail. 

 42. The concerned Senior Judicial Magistrate is directed to proceed with the case in accordance with law.
